Stressors and their families: daily hassles, major life events, chronic strain
Fight-or-flight response, named and attributed to Walter Cannon
General adaptation syndrome: alarm, resistance, exhaustion (Selye)
Chronic stress and health: cumulative wear and tear, stated factually
Honest framing: stress as the body's alarm system — useful and expensive

claims.claim: Stress is the body's response to demands or threats; response-based definitions conceptualize stress chiefly as the body's physiological reaction to any demand placed on it.

Hans Selye, the endocrinologist who pioneered stress research, defined stress as the response of the body to any demand, whether caused by pleasant or unpleasant conditions (Selye, 1976); the APA Dictionary credits Selye with first describing stress in psychology around 1940.
A stressor is any event, force, or condition that results in physical or emotional stress.

Stressors include daily hassles — minor irritations that build on one another and can leave people as stressed as major events (Kanner et al., 1981) — major life events requiring significant readjustment (Holmes & Rahe, 1967), and chronic stressors that persist over an extended period.

Walter Cannon, a Harvard physiologist, first articulated and named the fight-or-flight response (Cannon, 1932): a pattern of sympathetic nervous system arousal — increased heart and breathing rate, pupil dilation, blood flow to skeletal muscles — that mobilizes the body to fight or flee a perceived threat.

The fight-or-flight machinery is ancient and tuned for physical emergencies; most modern stressors do not call for fighting or fleeing, so the body's alarm often rings with no physical action to match — presented as an honest interpretive framing, not a research statistic.

Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome (GAS) describes three stages of responding to prolonged stress: the alarm reaction (immediate mobilization, roughly the fight-or-flight response), the stage of resistance (adaptation while remaining on alert with reduced intensity), and the stage of exhaustion (depleted resources, failing adaptation, greater vulnerability to illness) (Selye, 1936; 1976).

Chronic or frequently excessive stress reactions produce cumulative wear and tear on the body (McEwen, 1998): sustained elevated cortisol can weaken immune functioning, and prolonged strain-related high blood pressure can take a toll on the heart.

Not all stress is harmful: Selye (1974) called the beneficial kind eustress (Greek eu, 'good') — the positive stress response from challenging but attainable tasks, generating fulfillment and high performance — as distinct from distress, the overwhelming kind.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Stimulus-based versus response-based definitions of stress
positions: Stimulus-based views define stress by external events that place demands on a person (e.g., Holmes and Rahe's life-event checklist)

Response-based views define stress as the body's reaction to any demand (Selye); appraisal-based views add that stress occurs when an event is interpreted as harmful and as exceeding available resources
conflictingEvidence.resolution: OpenStax notes neither stimulus-based nor response-based definitions alone are complete. This lesson uses the response-based working definition (attributed to Selye) and notes the appraisal point in passing ('stress is largely in the eye of the beholder'), without taking sides in the theoretical dispute.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do daily hassles or major life events matter more for stress?
positions: Major life events require significant readjustment and correlate with later illness (Holmes & Rahe, 1967)

Daily hassles build up and can leave people just as stressed as major events (Kanner et al., 1981); the Social Readjustment Rating Scale has been criticized for ignoring individual appraisal of events
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both as real stressor families without ranking them, and makes no quantitative claim about their relative impact. The Holmes and Rahe checklist appears only as historical background for the major-life-events family.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft made no verifiable factual claims about stress; statements such as 'Stress is a foundational concept in Psychology' and 'College courses use stress as a building block' are generic boilerplate and were discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the draft's boilerplate with a source-verified lesson: the working definition is attributed to Hans Selye, fight-or-flight to Walter Cannon, the three GAS stages to Selye, and eustress/distress to Selye; all examples, scenarios, and practice questions are original; no statistics were invented.
The draft's banned boilerplate phrases ('a college-level explanation names the concept', 'label on a toolbox drawer') were removed.

sourceRecords.title: Psychology 2e, Section 14.1: What Is Stress?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Canonical openstax.org URL registered; openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so the section was read via an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/2024id_/) of the canonical URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: response-based definitions of stress and Selye's definition of stress as the response of the body to any demand (Selye, 1976); Cannon's articulation and naming of the fight-or-flight response (Cannon, 1932) with sympathetic and endocrine arousal; eustress and distress terminology (Selye, 1974); the three stages of the general adaptation syndrome (Selye, 1936; 1976) — alarm reaction, stage of resistance, stage of exhaustion; the appraisal point that stress is largely in the eye of the beholder. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: APA Dictionary of Psychology — stress
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API (getdopdefinitions on the published apiPath). Definition: the physiological or psychological response to internal or external stressors, involving changes affecting nearly every system of the body; entry notes stress was first described in the context of psychology around 1940 by Hans Selye. Supports the working definition and the Selye attribution. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: APA Dictionary of Psychology — fight-or-flight response
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API. Definition: a pattern of physiological changes elicited by sympathetic nervous system activity in response to threatening situations, mobilizing energy for physical activity (increased heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure; pupil dilation; blood flow routed to skeletal muscles); entry records it was first described by Walter B. Cannon. Supports the fight-or-flight subsection and its attribution. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: APA Dictionary of Psychology — general adaptation syndrome (GAS)
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API. Definition: the physiological consequences of severe stress, with three stages — alarm (including the shock and countershock phases, with sympathetic arousal and the fight-or-flight response), resistance (stabilization at increased physiological levels), and exhaustion. Supports the GAS subsection. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: APA Dictionary of Psychology — eustress
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API. Definition: the positive stress response involving optimal levels of stimulation, from challenging but attainable and enjoyable or worthwhile tasks, with a beneficial effect on fulfillment, growth, and performance; entry records it was first described by Hans Selye. Supports the eustress subsection. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: APA Dictionary of Psychology — stressor
sourceRecords.provider: American Psychological Association (APA Dictionary of Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Entry read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public content API. Definition: any event, force, or condition that results in physical or emotional stress, internal or external. Supports the stressor definition used in the lesson and the vocabulary entry. Paraphrased only.
